# Review without a queue: what Chen and Stratton (2026) mean for an autonomous system

> Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.

## Abstract

Fiona Chen, James Stratton (Harvard University): AI coding tools raise code output substantially but final software output only a little, with no detectable employment effect. Code review becomes the bottleneck: code waits longer for a reviewer, spends longer in review and draws more requested changes. We map each of their findings to the mechanisms Ultrastable uses instead of a human review queue, and test each mapping against this system's own records. 5 of 7 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## The study

Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production. Fiona Chen, James Stratton, Harvard University; job market paper (working paper, not peer reviewed), version 2026-11-19 (first version 2026-01-07). Data: 445M work events (GitHub, Jira, Google Calendar) for 720,542 workers at 655 firms, January 2021 to August 2026, from an engineering analytics platform; staggered difference-in-differences on AI tool adoption timing.

## Findings, mechanisms and measurements

### F1. More code is not more shipped work (economics)

**The study:** After AI agent adoption, pull requests opened rise 35.7% while resolved issues (work deployed to production) rise only 13.7%; increases above 30.7% are ruled out. (Introduction; conclusion)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- CRITICALITY-1 (`foundation/criticality.py`): the system's own score counts verified live deploys, never commits or lines
- PROGRESS-1 (`site/progress.js`): the public progress page lists merged and shipped work only; record-keeping merges are excluded

**Measured here:** verified live deploys per merged pull request in the same window: 0.625 (n = 64). Target >= 0.5. Verdict: **met**.
Source: ops/deploys.jsonl and the pull request snapshot.

### F2. Review becomes the bottleneck (economics)

**The study:** After AI agent adoption, the time from a pull request's submission to its merge rises 56.1%: waiting for a reviewer rises 59.9% and time in active review 58.5%. (Introduction; section on review)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1 (`seed/worker/src/sweeper.js`): a server-side lane merges a green pull request without waiting for a person
- HANDOFF-1 (`seed/worker/src/handoff.js`): the tick Worker owns merge, deploy and live verification after a pull request opens
- DRAIN-ZERO-1 (`foundation/lanewatch.py`): a green pull request left open fails a check

**Measured here:** median hours from a pull request opening to its merge: 0.15 (n = 64). Target <= 1.0. Verdict: **met**.
Source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 100 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-21T09:30:00Z.

### F3. System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones (economics)

**The study:** The study's model predicts that when review capacity is fixed, the waiting time grows with the volume of submitted code. A system that writes its own changes must not let its own pull requests queue behind human-driven ones. (Model, propositions on backlog and wait time)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- DRAIN-ALL-1 (`.github/workflows/lane.yml`): the lane takes every open pull request until none is left
- SELF-REFERENCE-1 (`foundation/criticality.py`): work the system originates on itself is ranked first when the regime is driven

**Measured here:** median hours to merge for pull requests the system's own workflows or App opened: 0.49 (n = 13). Target <= 2.0. Verdict: **met**.
Source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 100 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-21T09:30:00Z.

### F4. Lower code quality raises review effort and risk (quality)

**The study:** After agent adoption the share of changes receiving a review comment rises 13.1% and comments per change rise 38.6%; interviewees report outages caused by AI-generated commits. (Introduction; interviews)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- ELISION-1 (`foundation/executor.py`): a model change that elides or stubs code is refused before it becomes a pull request
- REDMAIN-1 (`foundation/redmain.py`): a red main is repaired by reverting the smallest change that broke it
- FAILURE-RESOLVE-1 (`foundation/failure_audit.py`): every failure mode has a live detector and a queue item

**Measured here:** commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window: 0.0 (n = 64). Target <= 0.05. Verdict: **met**.
Source: git log of main, subjects starting with Revert.

### F5. Unverified deploys reach production (quality)

**The study:** Code must be reviewed and tested before it can be deployed; the study treats review as the quality gate that AI-written code strains. (Introduction)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- HANDOFF-1 (`seed/worker/src/handoff.js`): every deploy runs a verify line against production and rolls back on failure
- FRONT-BACKED-1 (`site/live.js`): freshness of each live source is served and probed

**Measured here:** share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit: 1.0 (n = 40). Target >= 0.95. Verdict: **met**.
Source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window).

### F6. AI review tools leave humans in the loop (oversight)

**The study:** 79.1% of firms adopted AI code review tools, but the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments are still written by people, so the bottleneck persists. (Introduction)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- CLOSED-LOOP-1 (`foundation/closedloop.py`): no step waits on a person reading, reviewing or approving
- CRITICALITY-1 (`foundation/criticality.py`): human touches are counted every tick and lower the score

**Measured here:** share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself: 0.203 (n = 64). Target >= 0.5. Verdict: **not-met**. Open item: `Q-RES-chen-stratton-2026-F6`.
Source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 100 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-21T09:30:00Z.

### F7. One approver is a single point of failure (oversight)

**The study:** Reviewers mostly review code they already know (82.8% versus 17.2% at random); an interviewee describes one senior engineer as the only approver, reviewing once a week. (Introduction; interviews)

**How Ultrastable answers it:**

- GUIDING-DIRECTIVE section 12 (`doctrine/registers.json`): every single point of failure, approvals included, is registered and remediated
- NO-SINGLE-ROUTE (`foundation/failover.py`): every merge and deploy path has a second route needing no person's credential

**Measured here:** verified deploys the system originated and executed itself (latest criticality tick): 0 (n = 0). Target >= 1. Verdict: **not-met**. Open item: `Q-RES-chen-stratton-2026-F7`.
Source: ops/criticality.jsonl at 2026-11-24T17:40:23Z.

## Limits

- Scale. One organization: 100 closed pull requests (64 merged) over 0.75 days, against a study of 655 firms over more than five years. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 80% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Job market paper (working paper, not peer reviewed), version 2026-11-19 (first version 2026-01-07); its findings may change in later versions.

## Method

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history.
